newsitem.title: INDIA: India finance cos under strain after CRB crash.
newsitem.headline: India finance cos under strain after CRB crash.

text.p: Indian authorities on Friday said they would complete within a month an investigation into the failed CRB group of companies, accused of irregularities in financial services and whose liabilities are estimated at 9.32 billion rupees ($260 million).
"The investigations are expected to be completed in one month's time," Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) director Joginder Singh told reporters.
Singh's comments came as industry officials on Friday reported growing requests for refunds from non-bank finance companies (NBFCs) by small investors, shaken by the CRB fiasco.
"Requests for refunds have almost doubled in the case of some companies in Bombay," said an executive of a Bombay finance firm who did not want to be identified.
Last week, the Reserve Bank of India, charged CRB Capital Markets, which has offices in India and abroad, with a series of irregularities relating to its activities.
Newspapers reported how depositors became anxious after company cheques bounced or officials were unavailable for clarification.
The CBI on Thursday raided the Bombay residence of CRB chairman Chain Roop Bhansali, who police said was absconding. The firm's offices were earlier raided by the authorities.

The CBI's Singh, who gave the figure of estimated liabilities, said money was owed to the Gujarat state government, participants of the inter-corporate deposit market and the public who invested deposits in flagship CRB Capital Markets Ltd and in the group's mutual fund.
Analysts said the crisis had triggered an erosion of confidence in finance companies.
"NBFCs - especially those in Ahmedabad and other parts of Gujarat - are facing redemption pressure," S.R. Krishnan, banking and finance analyst at Peregrine Capital India said.
On Friday, Kotak Mahindra Finance Company, a leading NBFC, on Friday in an advertisement in the Times of India newspaper sought to allay investors' apprehensions on deposit programmes.
"A lot of people are suddently asking all manner of questions about fixed deposits (FDs)," the advertisement said.
"They are even questioning whether it's okay to invest in FDs anymore," it said. "It is about time someone came up with the answers."
Without referring to the CRB crisis, Kotak Mahindra Finance said investors should not generalise but look at each company's credentials.
It urged investors to check safety ratings on NBFC's FD issues and to balance returns with safety and service.
"There is a lot of confusion among investors which we wanted to clear," a Kotak Mahindra official told Reuters.
He said his company was not facing any redemption pressure.
"I am sure some amount of shift is happening," Peregrine's Krishnan said about investors switching deposits from NBFCs to banks despite the lower interest banks pay on term deposits.
"NBFCs from reputed business houses like the Tatas will not be affected," said an executive at a leading NBFC.
"Even if there is a run, they could borrow and pay investors. But the lesser known ones will be hit," he said.
He said well-known NBFCs in the southern state of Tamil Nadu, where the industry is well established, were not facing any redemption pressure from investors.
The Reserve Bank of India on Thursday invited claims from investors of CRB Capital Markets for submission to the official liquidator appointed by the Delhi High Court.
A winding up petition filed by the Reserve Bank of India will be heard on July 22.
The RBI had earlier withdrawn an in-principle permission given to the company to set up a private bank.
